**Title:** Same Name, Different Unit: Identifying Source-Specific Units in Web Price Fusion

**Abstract (268 words):**

Crypto prices are commonly quoted in dollars, but an exchange's dollar balance is a claim on that exchange and may not be worth a redeemable U.S. dollar. When banking access is impaired, its ledger dollar can trade at a discount, and price services that combine quotes across exchanges then read a change in the dollar as a change in price. We develop an hourly method that separates exchange-specific dollar shifts from asset-specific price movements. The price gap shared by all assets on an exchange estimates its dollar offset, and a stablecoin traded there, netted of its price on an outside exchange, tests whether that offset is a unit shift or demand for the assets. We apply the method from 2017 to 2025. On Bitfinex from November 2018 to May 2019, the netted stablecoin tracked the dollar offset with slope 0.97 (0.94 to 1.00), a reading earlier work could not test. Binance.US in 2023 gave 1.00. A pre-registered panel of eight local-currency units on three exchanges gave a pooled 0.978 (0.962 to 0.989), partly reflecting arbitrage within each exchange, and a second exchange gave 1.005; placebos that mismatch the currency gave slopes near 0.145. These shifts distort aggregated prices: converting local-currency markets at official rates erred by 128.1 basis points against 6.8 through the exchange's own stablecoin, and the median of officially converted markets by 107.4 against 5.4. Where most trading shared a stablecoin that lost its peg, a frozen unit-aware method beat the median and two standard fusion methods out of sample. By identifying which unit of account has moved, the method makes cross-exchange crypto prices more interpretable.

**Suggested keywords:** exchange dollars; unit of account; truth discovery; price feeds and oracles; Web data quality; cryptocurrency markets; reproducibility
